a1.say: Let's solve Find a Peak, using the Binary Search on the Slope approach.

card.title: Find a Peak
card.sub: Binary Search on the Slope · Medium

a1.cap: A peak is a value strictly greater than its neighbours (treat outside the array as −∞). Adjacent values are never equal. Return the index of any peak in O(log n). For this exercise the input has exactly one peak.
a1.say: A peak is a value strictly greater than its neighbours (treat outside the array as minus infinity ). Adjacent values are never equal. Return the index of any peak in O of log n. For this exercise the input has exactly one peak.

lines: A peak is a value strictly greater than its neighbours (treat outside the array as −∞). Adjacent values are never equal. Return the index of any peak in O(log n). For this exercise the input has exactly one peak.

a1.cap: For example, with nums = [1,2,3,1], the answer is 2.
a1.say: For example, with nums equals 1, 2, 3, 1, the answer is 2.

a1.cap: Look at the middle and its right neighbour. If the slope goes up, there must be a peak to the right; if it goes down, a peak is at mid or to the left. Halve the range accordingly.
Let's walk through it with nums = [1,2,3,1].
a1.say: Let's walk through it with nums equals 1, 2, 3, 1.

a1.cap: Uphill from 2 to 3: a peak is to the right.
Downhill after 3: a peak is here or to the left.
Time complexity is O(log n) and extra space is O(1).
a1.say: Time complexity is O of log n and extra space is O of one.

a1.cap: That's the Binary Search on the Slope approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
